questions.q: Why is a trie a natural fit for prefix matching?
options: It stores strings hashed, giving O(1) exact-match lookups
It automatically keeps all stored entries ordered by their popularity scores
Walking from the root by each character reaches all completions of a prefix
It compresses queries better than any inverted index
questions.explanation: A trie encodes shared prefixes as shared paths, so walking one node per character lands on the subtree containing exactly the matching completions. Hashing gives exact-match lookups only, not prefix enumeration.

questions.q: What does 'top-k suggestions' mean in autocomplete?
options: Return the k highest-scoring completions for the typed prefix
Return the k terms that were most recently inserted into the index
Return k random completions to diversify the results
Return the k shortest completions that match the prefix
questions.explanation: Top-k means ranking all completions of the prefix by a relevance score (usually frequency plus recency) and returning the best k, since a UI can only show a handful.

questions.q: Roughly what end-to-end latency budget does keystroke autocomplete target?
options: Around 2 seconds, hidden by a loading spinner
Around 100 milliseconds or less, so suggestions feel instant
Around 1 millisecond, requiring on-device inference
Around 500 milliseconds, comparable to a typical full page load
questions.explanation: Suggestions must land before the next keystroke to feel instant, which puts the budget near 100ms. A millisecond is unattainable over a network round trip, and half a second reads as visibly laggy.

questions.q: Why is caching so effective for autocomplete traffic?
options: Suggestions never change, so caches never need invalidation
Browsers cache responses, so servers see little traffic
Autocomplete responses are very large, so caching saves substantial bandwidth
Prefix popularity is highly skewed; a few prefixes dominate requests
questions.explanation: Query prefixes follow a Zipf-like distribution, so a small hot set absorbs most traffic and a modest cache yields very high hit rates. Suggestions do change, so caches still need TTLs.

questions.q: Where do suggestion candidates usually come from?
options: Aggregated historical query logs weighted by frequency and recency
Live crawling of the result pages while users type each character
Manual curation of every phrase by a taxonomy team
Random walks over a knowledge graph seeded per session
questions.explanation: What real users actually searched is the best predictor of what the next user wants, so candidates are mined from aggregated query logs and scored by frequency and recency. Manual curation cannot scale to billions of phrases.

questions.q: What client-side technique cuts request volume while typing?
options: Retrying each keystroke request until it succeeds
Opening one request for every character over separate parallel connections
Prefetching the full dictionary on page load
Debouncing: waiting briefly after a keystroke before querying
questions.explanation: Debouncing waits out a short pause (roughly 50-100ms) so a burst of fast keystrokes produces one request instead of many, cutting load without a latency cost the user notices.

questions.q: Why precompute and store top-k completions per prefix instead of ranking at query time?
options: Ranking at query time returns unstable, flickering suggestion lists
Precomputation removes the need to store raw query logs
It turns each request into a cheap lookup within the latency budget
Search engines cannot sort by score during a live request
questions.explanation: Traversing a subtree and sorting candidates per keystroke is too slow at scale; precomputing shifts that work offline so serving becomes a single key lookup that fits the ~100ms budget.

questions.q: What is a compressed (radix/Patricia) trie's advantage over a plain trie?
options: It natively supports fuzzy matching operations at every internal node
Chains of single-child nodes collapse, cutting memory and hops
It stores scores in leaves, which plain tries cannot
It rebalances automatically as popular terms shift
questions.explanation: A radix trie merges each chain of single-child nodes into one edge labeled with the whole substring, so it stores far fewer node objects and traverses fewer pointers per lookup.

questions.q: Typo tolerance ('bierber' to 'bieber') is usually implemented how at scale?
options: Running full Levenshtein against every dictionary term per keystroke
Asking users to confirm their spelling before querying
Storing every possible misspelling of every term in the trie
Fuzzy candidates via edit-distance automata or precomputed variants on a bounded set
questions.explanation: Bounded edit-distance automata (or deletion-variant tables) generate only candidates within one or two edits, keeping work small. Scanning every dictionary term per keystroke is far too slow.

questions.q: New trending queries ('earthquake now') must surface within minutes. Pure daily batch rebuilds fail this. What's the standard architecture?
options: A small real-time layer over recent logs merged with the batch-built index
Rebuilding the entire trie from scratch every sixty seconds
Letting editorial staff manually inject trending phrases through an admin console
Ranking purely by recency so new queries always outrank old ones
questions.explanation: A lambda-style split keeps the large, stable index on a batch cadence while a small streaming layer over recent logs is merged at serve time, giving minute-level freshness cheaply.

questions.q: Autocomplete for a 100M-term index must be sharded. Sharding by first letter causes what problem?
options: Prefix queries must fan out to every shard and merge
Terms can no longer be ranked consistently across shard boundaries
Extremely uneven load, since letters differ hugely in traffic
The trie cannot be split without breaking parent pointers
questions.explanation: Letter frequencies are wildly skewed, so the 's' shard gets orders of magnitude more terms and traffic than 'z', creating hotspots. Routing itself works fine, which is why fan-out is not the issue.

questions.q: Users in Japan see suggestions ranked for US traffic. What design choice most directly fixes relevance?
options: Translating the US suggestion list into Japanese at serve time
Per-region (and per-language) indexes and ranking models
A global model with users' IPs appended as ranking features at serve time
Serving all suggestions from the geographically nearest datacenter
questions.explanation: Relevance comes from the candidate pool, so building indexes from each region's own query logs fixes it at the source. A nearby datacenter only improves latency, not what is suggested.

questions.q: The suggestion service goes down. What is the correct degradation for the search page?
options: Block the search box until the service recovers
Fail open: plain typing works, suggestions just don't appear
Queue keystrokes and replay them once the service returns
Redirect users to a cached static copy of the results page
questions.explanation: Autocomplete is a convenience layered on search, so its failure must never block the core flow; the box stays usable and suggestions silently disappear.

questions.q: Suggestions must exclude offensive or policy-violating phrases. Where is the filter best applied primarily?
options: Client-side, in JavaScript, against a downloaded blocklist
At the CDN, by pattern-matching response bodies
At index build time, so blocked phrases never enter the candidate set
Post-serving, by retracting suggestions after user reports
questions.explanation: Filtering during the offline build means banned phrases are never stored or served, costs nothing at request time, and cannot be bypassed. Client-side blocklists are visible and trivially skipped.

questions.q: Keystroke responses can arrive out of order ('ca' results after 'cat' results). How do clients prevent stale lists?
options: Tag requests with the typed string or sequence and drop stale responses
Use a single persistent connection so response ordering is guaranteed end to end
Add server delays so responses always return in request order
Disable suggestions while any request remains in flight
questions.explanation: The client stamps each request with the prefix or a monotonic sequence number and renders a response only if it matches the current input, discarding late arrivals from older keystrokes.

questions.q: Prefix hit rates in the CDN drop sharply for longer prefixes. Why?
options: CDNs cap key length, evicting longer prefix entries first
Longer prefixes produce larger responses that exceed cache limits
TTLs shrink automatically as the cache key length grows
Longer prefixes are more unique, so requests rarely repeat
questions.explanation: The space of possible prefixes grows exponentially with length, so long prefixes are nearly unique per user and rarely requested twice before eviction, leaving nothing to hit.

questions.q: In a precomputed-table design storing top-8 completions for prefixes up to 6 characters, what dominates memory?
options: The number of distinct prefixes times the stored top-k lists
The raw historical query logs retained in memory for ranking every entry
The HTTP response templates cached per suggestion
Checksum metadata verifying each list's integrity
questions.explanation: Every distinct observed prefix gets its own materialized list of 8 strings, so footprint is roughly prefix count times k times average suggestion size. Raw logs live offline, not in the serving tier.

questions.q: Edge caches hold hot prefixes; origin holds the full index. A celebrity scandal makes a cold prefix hot instantly. Main risk and mitigation?
options: Cache poisoning; sign every suggestion payload at the origin
Origin stampede on the miss; coalesce requests and warm caches on trend detection
Shard imbalance; re-hash the entire prefix space each hour
Stale ranking; shorten every TTL to one second globally
questions.explanation: A simultaneous miss on one key sends the whole surge to origin; request coalescing collapses it to a single fetch, and proactive warming on trend signals fills edges before the spike.

questions.q: Personalized autocomplete (user history biases ranking) conflicts with edge caching. Which architecture reconciles them?
options: Cache per-user suggestion lists at the edge keyed by user ID
Disable caching entirely whenever any user is logged in
Move all personalization into the browser's local history only
Cache generic top-k at the edge; re-rank lightly with user context at the client or app tier
questions.explanation: Splitting the work keeps the expensive, shareable candidate generation cacheable while the cheap personal re-rank happens per user, so hit rates stay high. Per-user cache keys destroy sharing entirely.

questions.q: You must bound tail latency: p99 under 80ms even when a shard is slow. Which technique targets exactly this?
options: Raising the connection pool size to that shard
Retrying failed requests up to five times with backoff
Hedged requests: send a duplicate to a replica after a short delay
Caching each previous response and always serving it before querying shards
questions.explanation: Hedging fires a second copy to a replica once a request exceeds, say, the p95 mark and takes whichever returns first, cutting the tail for a few percent extra load. Retries only help after a failure, too late for p99.
